RewardsCompetitionsNewslettersWeather ForecastUKBurnham begins to unpick Brexit with landmark dealBrussels agreement  ‘will only take us so far’, says British prime ministerEuropean Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, Britain's prime minister Andy Burnham and European Council president Antonio Costa join hands after a press conference following a EU-UK Summit. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images Andy Bounds in BrusselsGeorge Parker and Peter Foster in LondonFri Nov 20 2026 - 14:29 • 4 MIN READBritish prime minister Andy Burnham began unpicking Brexit by agreeing a landmark deal on Friday with the EU, but the summit in Brussels was overshadowed by a dispute over university tuition fees and questions about where the partnership goes next.

Burnham said the deal, which removed barriers to trade in food and drink and created a new youth experience scheme, was “good for Britain and good for Europe” and claimed that fresh Treasury analysis suggested it could boost UK GDP by 0.5 per cent.

But Burnham, who has raised the prospect of the UK rejoining the EU, conceded that the Brussels deal was insufficient for the long term. “Incremental steps will only take us so far,” he said.

The prime minister has promised a national debate on “options” for future EU-UK relations but tried to kick that discussion down the track until the next summit with the EU, probably in autumn 2027.

“We will have an informal brainstorming process to assess what the options are,” he said at a joint press conference with European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen. He said any decisions would be for the next parliament.

[ Zombie nation: Burnham’s Britain ponders its Brexit woesOpens in new window ]

But in a bruising reminder of the political dangers of trying to unravel Brexit – and the perils of negotiations with the EU – Burnham was surprised to find his deal put on ice by the bloc’s 27 member states.

They stipulated on Friday morning that the three agreements, which also included a deal to link carbon markets, would only be implemented if Britain agreed within six months to charge lower “home fees” for European students studying at UK universities.

On a day of briefings and counter-briefings, Burnham insisted: “I don’t think there’s any confusion at all. The deal is done.”

Britain has offered to reduce fees but not to the same level as domestic students. Complying with the EU request would cost the UK hundreds of millions of pounds a year.

“This is a great deal for the UK, getting what they asked for,” an EU diplomat said of Friday’s agreement. “But for some countries there’s nothing to gain from this deal. They need tuition fee cuts to make it balanced,” they added.

[ Andy Burnham will sign a Brexit reset deal tomorrow. The real battle comes nextOpens in new window ]

Under the youth scheme expected to start in 2030, each side would offer 100,000 visas a year to young people to work and study in each other’s countries. The linking of emissions trading systems would avoid carbon border taxes across the Channel.

The two sides also pledged closer co-operation on defence and combating irregular migration.

However, there was little progress on UK demands to be included in emerging “made in Europe” policies that would exclude British companies from some industrial subsidies and procurement contracts because they are outside the bloc’s single market.

Burnham said he would introduce a landmark bill next week that would allow EU laws to, in effect, be copied and pasted into the British statute book.

The deal had been unlocked a day earlier after France watered down its opposition to giving Britain a say in “shaping” new EU rules on food standards that will apply in the UK.

British officials will now be able to observe meetings on implementing the rules but not vote on them. They can also be invited to attend meetings preparing to respond to “emergencies” such as animal disease outbreaks.

Burnham denied it was a “fig leaf”, adding: “It’s quite a moment, actually, to have British experts back in the room.”

But 18 months of gruelling negotiations that finished in the early hours of Friday left EU member states’ appetite for more mini deals “finished”, four EU diplomats told the Financial Times.

They said Burnham now needed to commit to a full negotiation on joining a customs union, the single market or full membership of the EU.

“[The British] need to tell us which status they want, and then we can work on how to make that happen,” said one.

“It’s a pain,” said a second diplomat, adding that the UK sought to be “in and out at the same time”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

[ Andy Burnham wants the UK back in the EU. But does Ireland?Opens in new window ]

The UK has offered a discount while the EU continues to demand that its students pay the same as UK students. Details are expected to be hammered out in the next six months.

The deal will include Britain offering 100,000 visas a year to young people aged 18-31 to work and study in the UK – the UK originally offered 50,000 – as part of a reciprocal deal with EU member states.

France agreed to give British experts a say in shaping new EU laws on food standards – but not a vote.

Burnham will emphasise a part of the deal that will see more co-operation on tackling illicit migration, a key domestic issue.

The EU and UK will deepen their co-operation on security and defence issues as a key part of a closer relationship, specifically focusing on maritime security, countering hybrid threats and support to Ukraine.

– Copyright The Financial Times Limited
